html:
William of Rubruck was a Flemish Franciscan friar who travelled to the court of the Mongol great khan Möngke and reached Karakorum in the spring of 1254. He wrote his report for King Louis IX of France. It holds the first detailed European description of the capital of the Mongol Empire. Here he describes the silver drinking fountain at the khan's palace, and then the city.

In the entry of this great palace, it being unseemly to bring in there skins of milk and other drinks, master William the Parisian had made for him a great silver tree, and at its roots are four lions of silver, each with a conduit through it, and all belching forth white milk of mares. And four conduits are led inside the tree to its tops, which are bent downward, and on each of these is also a gilded serpent, whose tail twines round the tree. And from one of these pipes flows wine, from another caracosmos, or clarified mare's milk, from another bal, a drink made with honey, and from another rice mead, which is called terracina …
Of the city of Caracarum you must know that, exclusive of the palace of the Chan, it is not as big as the village of Saint Denis, and the monastery of Saint Denis is ten times larger than the palace. There are two quarters in it; one of the Saracens in which are the markets, … the other is the quarter of the Cathayans, all of whom are artisans.
